accepted.s: The annual publication titled “Energy Statistics” is brought out by which organisation?
o: Central Electricity Authority under the Ministry of Power
Central Statistics Office, now functioning as the National Statistics Office under MoSPI
accepted.x: Energy Statistics was published by the Central Statistics Office (CSO), now the National Statistics Office (NSO) under MoSPI.
accepted.tq: Identify the correct publishing authority rather than a related sectoral body.
accepted.sec: Energy Statistics India - publisher and indicators

accepted.s: Which one of the following is NOT covered by the publication “Energy Statistics”?
o: Energy production and imports or exports
Reserves and potential of energy resources
accepted.x: Energy Statistics covers reserves and potential, installed capacity, production, imports and exports, consumption and energy balance for major energy sources. Literacy and school-enrolment data are outside its stated coverage.
accepted.tq: Find the unrelated indicator among otherwise closely connected sectoral measures.
accepted.sec: Energy Statistics India - publisher and indicators

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the coverage of Energy Statistics:
1. It includes data on coal, lignite, crude oil and natural gas.
2. It includes electricity consumption and the energy balance.
3. It is restricted to production data and excludes imports and exports.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the publication also covers imports and exports.
accepted.tq: Locate the false exclusion statement by checking the publication’s full range of indicators.
accepted.sec: Energy Statistics India - publisher and indicators

accepted.s: India’s per-capita energy consumption increased from 15,296 MJ in 2016 to which value in 2025?
accepted.x: Per-capita energy consumption rose from 15,296 MJ in 2016 to 18,096 MJ in 2025.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the reported endpoint from nearby numerical distractors.
accepted.sec: Energy Statistics India - publisher and indicators

accepted.s: The approximate compound annual growth rate of India’s per-capita energy consumption from 2016 to 2025 was:
accepted.x: The reported CAGR for the increase from 15,296 MJ to 18,096 MJ was about 1.89%.
accepted.tq: Read the growth-rate figure independently of the starting and ending values.
accepted.sec: Energy Statistics India - publisher and indicators

accepted.s: India’s per-capita electricity consumption increased from 957 kWh in FY 2014 to approximately what level in FY 2025?
accepted.x: Per-capita electricity consumption rose from 957 kWh in FY 2014 to 1,460 kWh in FY 2025.
accepted.tq: Use the time labels carefully and select the correct terminal value.
accepted.sec: Per-capita energy and electricity consumption - world gap, HDI link

accepted.s: India’s per-capita energy consumption is approximately what fraction of the world average?
accepted.x: India’s per-capita energy consumption is reported as only one-third of the world average.
accepted.tq: Separate the current world-gap ratio from older references to one-half of the world average.
accepted.sec: Per-capita energy and electricity consumption - world gap, HDI link

accepted.s:
With reference to per-capita electricity generation in 2024, consider the following statements:
1. India recorded 1,418 kWh.
2. China recorded 7,097 kWh.
3. The United States recorded 12,701 kWh.
4. The OECD average was a little above 8,000 kWh.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All four statements correctly reproduce the 2024 comparison: India 1,418 kWh, China 7,097 kWh, the USA 12,701 kWh and the OECD average a little above 8,000 kWh.
accepted.tq: Verify every row of a comparison table before choosing the all-inclusive option.
accepted.sec: Per-capita energy and electricity consumption - world gap, HDI link

accepted.s: In 2024, India’s per-capita energy consumption was 7,893 kWh. This implies that approximately what share of total energy use was electricity?
accepted.x: The reported comparison indicates that only about one-fifth of India’s energy use was electricity in 2024.
accepted.tq: Convert the stated comparison into the corresponding fraction rather than confusing energy with electricity.
accepted.sec: Per-capita energy and electricity consumption - world gap, HDI link

accepted.s: The policy objective of raising per-capita electricity consumption is linked to the Human Development Index primarily because:
o: Electricity consumption is unrelated to social development indicators
Higher electricity consumption automatically eliminates urban-rural disparity
A minimum level of per-capita consumption is needed for a minimally acceptable level of well-being
HDI measures only the availability of commercial energy
accepted.x: Per-capita electricity consumption acts as a proxy for energy use, and a certain minimum level is required to ensure a minimally acceptable level of well-being.
accepted.tq: Apply the development-indicator relationship to the policy objective.
accepted.sec: Per-capita energy and electricity consumption - world gap, HDI link

accepted.s: Which one of the following best describes the pattern of India’s per-capita energy consumption?
o: High per-capita consumption with negligible regional disparity
High rural consumption with negligible urban consumption
Low per-capita consumption accompanied by a large urban-rural disparity
Uniform consumption across urban and rural areas
accepted.x: India has low per-capita consumption and a large disparity between urban and rural areas.
accepted.tq: Use the paired qualifiers—low level and large disparity—to identify the precise description.
accepted.sec: Per-capita energy and electricity consumption - world gap, HDI link

accepted.s: Which source supplies approximately 55% of India’s energy mix and over 74% of its power generation?
accepted.x: Coal supplies about 55% of the energy mix and more than 74% of power generation.
accepted.tq: Match the quantitative share with the correct fuel source.
accepted.sec: Fuel-wise share of primary energy - ranking of sources

accepted.s: Fossil fuels constitute nearly what proportion of India’s commercial primary energy supply?
accepted.x: Fossil fuels account for nearly 90% of India’s commercial primary energy supply.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the commercial primary-energy share from the separate coal shares.
accepted.sec: Fuel-wise share of primary energy - ranking of sources

accepted.s:
Arrange the following sources in descending order of installed power capacity in 2026, after coal:
A. Wind
B. Large hydro
C. Solar
D. Oil and gas
accepted.x: After coal, the order was solar, wind, large hydro, and oil and gas. Their capacities were approximately 157 GW, 56.8 GW, 52 GW and 20.7 GW respectively.
accepted.tq: Rank the options by magnitude, beginning with the largest capacity after coal.
accepted.sec: Fuel-wise share of primary energy - ranking of sources

accepted.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding installed power capacity in 2026:

List-I (Source)
A. Solar
B. Wind
C. Nuclear
D. Small hydro

List-II (Capacity)
I. 5.18 GW
II. 8.78 GW
III. 56.8 GW
IV. 157 GW

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
accepted.x: Solar had 157 GW, wind 56.8 GW, nuclear 8.78 GW and small hydro 5.18 GW of installed capacity.
accepted.tq: Start from the distinctive capacity figures and eliminate codes with mismatched source-capacity pairs.
accepted.sec: Fuel-wise share of primary energy - ranking of sources

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly represents the order of the two largest sources of installed power capacity in 2026?
accepted.x: Coal was the largest source with 230 GW, followed by solar with 157 GW, approximately 29% of installed capacity.
accepted.tq: Test the ranking rather than confusing energy-mix share with installed-capacity order.
accepted.sec: Fuel-wise share of primary energy - ranking of sources

accepted.s: An energy crisis, in the sense used in discussions of conventional energy resources, refers to:
o: A rise in electricity consumption during solar hours
A temporary fall in renewable-energy generation only
The danger that fossil fuels such as coal and petroleum may run out
A shortage limited to nuclear fuel imports
accepted.x: Energy crisis refers to the danger of exhaustion of fossil fuels such as coal and petroleum.
accepted.tq: Identify the underlying resource-depletion meaning rather than a short-term grid event.
accepted.sec: Fuel-wise share of primary energy - ranking of sources

accepted.s: India is currently described as the world’s:
accepted.x: India is the third-largest energy consumer in the world.
accepted.tq: Recall the global rank directly and avoid confusing it with India’s coal-consumption rank.
accepted.sec: Primary energy demand - India's global rank

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly states India’s position in global coal consumption and the expected change in energy demand by 2047?
o: Second-largest coal consumer; demand is expected to triple
Largest coal consumer; demand is expected to double
Fourth-largest coal consumer; demand is expected to halve
Third-largest coal consumer; demand is expected to remain unchanged
accepted.x: India is the world’s second-largest coal consumer, and its energy demand is expected to triple by 2047.
accepted.tq: Keep the two separate global comparisons together without swapping the ranks or growth estimate.
accepted.sec: Primary energy demand - India's global rank

accepted.s: India’s peak power shortage declined from approximately 4.2% in 2014 to what level in 2025?
accepted.x: The peak shortage fell sharply from 4.2% in 2014 to 0.03% in 2025.
accepted.tq: Pay attention to the decimal placement in a near-zero deficit figure.
accepted.sec: Peak demand vs peak met - deficit trend (CEA)

accepted.s: Peak demand on an electricity grid is defined as:
o: The average power drawn over a full day
The highest power drawn in a 15-minute interval
The total electricity generated in a month
The maximum annual energy produced by renewable sources
accepted.x: Peak demand is the highest power drawn from the grid during a 15-minute interval.
accepted.tq: Distinguish instantaneous or interval-based peak power from aggregate energy generation.
accepted.sec: Peak demand vs peak met - deficit trend (CEA)

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding recorded peak demand met:
1. Peak demand met during solar hours in 2024 was 250 GW.
2. Peak demand met during non-solar hours in 2025 was 237 GW.
3. The 2025 non-solar figure was higher than the 2024 solar-hours figure.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the figures were 250 GW in 2024 solar hours and 237 GW in 2025 non-solar hours. Statement 3 is false because 237 GW is lower than 250 GW.
accepted.tq: Compare both the year-specific figures and the direction of the comparison.
accepted.sec: Peak demand vs peak met - deficit trend (CEA)

accepted.s: On 25 April 2026, India’s peak demand met was recorded at approximately 256.1 GW, of which about what proportion was met by renewable energy?
accepted.x: Peak demand met was 256.1 GW on 25 April 2026, and about one-third of it was met by renewable energy.
accepted.tq: Link the date and peak figure with the associated renewable-energy share.
accepted.sec: Peak demand vs peak met - deficit trend (CEA)

accepted.s: Which of the following statements correctly describes the peak demand recorded in May 2026?
o: It was 256.1 GW, about one-third above the 2019 level
It was 237 GW, about 90 GW below the 2019 level
It was 250 GW, about 20 GW above the 2019 level
It was 270.8 GW, about 90 GW above the 2019 level
accepted.x: The May 2026 peak demand was an all-time high of 270.8 GW, approximately 90 GW above the 2019 level.
accepted.tq: Match the all-time-high figure with its correctly stated historical comparison.
accepted.sec: Peak demand vs peak met - deficit trend (CEA)

accepted.s: On 25 April 2026, which of the following correctly describes the difference between solar and non-solar hours?
o: There was a shortage in solar hours but no shortage in non-solar hours
There was no shortage in solar hours, but non-solar hours recorded a 2% deficit equivalent to 4,243 MW
Non-solar hours recorded no deficit because renewable generation was one-third of demand
Both solar and non-solar hours recorded a 2% deficit
accepted.x: The grid had no shortage during solar hours, whereas non-solar hours had a 2% deficit, equal to 4,243 MW.
accepted.tq: Separate the solar-hours result from the non-solar-hours deficit instead of reversing the two.
accepted.sec: Peak demand vs peak met - deficit trend (CEA)

accepted.s: The evening peak has become central to India’s storage push primarily because:
o: Renewable energy cannot contribute during daylight hours
Coal supplies less than one-tenth of power generation
The remaining deficit occurs mainly during non-solar evening hours
Electricity demand is highest only during solar hours
accepted.x: Although solar-hour supply has improved, the non-solar evening peak still creates a deficit, making storage important for meeting that period’s demand.
accepted.tq: Infer the policy response from the timing of the remaining grid deficit.
accepted.sec: Peak demand vs peak met - deficit trend (CEA)
